source_records.title: A Survey of Link Prediction in Temporal Networks
source_records.abstract: Temporal networks have gained significant prominence in the past decade for modelling dynamic interactions within complex systems. A key challenge in this domain is Temporal Link Prediction (TLP), which aims to forecast future connections by analysing historical network structures across a range of applications. While existing surveys have addressed specific aspects of TLP, they typically lack a comprehensive framework that distinguishes between representation and inference methods, the two key ingredients of TLP. This survey bridges this gap by introducing a novel taxonomy that explicitly examines representation and inference in existing methods, providing a novel classification of approaches for TLP. We analyse how different representation techniques capture temporal and structural dynamics, examining their compatibility with various inference methods for link prediction tasks. Our taxonomy not only clarifies the methodological landscape but also reveals promising unexplored combinations of existing techniques. This taxonomy provides a systematic foundation for tackling emerging challenges in TLP, including model explainability and scalable architectures for complex temporal networks.

source_records.title: Self-supervised deep clustering for spammer group detection
source_records.abstract: E-commerce platforms face the issue of spammer groups that post many fraudulent reviews within a certain period. This practice misleads consumers and undermines fair competition among merchants. Researchers have proposed various methods to combat these spammers. However, these methods typically handle user feature representation and candidate group division independently, lacking an effective feedback mechanism between the two. Moreover, the vast discrepancy in the number of negative samples compared to positive samples in the data leads to reduced recognition accuracy in detection models, affecting the precision of detection outcomes. Therefore, we propose a spammer group detection method based on self-supervised deep clustering. Initially, the relationship between user review timing and product ratings is extracted from user review data, and user relevance is calculated and used as weights to construct a weighted user relationship graph. Subsequently, we integrate deep learning models with clustering algorithms to propose a self-supervised deep clustering model that jointly optimizes user representation and clustering distribution. This model employs graph and node autoencoders to capture global structural information and local preference information of user nodes, respectively, and designs a linear fusion method to enhance user feature representation. Additionally, we construct a reliable target distribution and introduce Kullback-Leibler(KL) divergence to form a self-supervised mechanism, continuously optimizing feature representation and clustering assignment to refine high-quality candidate groups. Finally, we propose an anomaly detection method based on the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), which designs a filtering mechanism to improve the detection efficiency of spammer groups. Experiments indicate that the proposed method outperforms baseline methods on the Amazon, Yelp, and YelpChi datasets.

source_records.title: CaTSCAN: Calculating Typed Subgraph Counts Analytically for Networks
source_records.abstract: Large graphs can be considered to be made of small subgraphs, called graphlets , that make up its fundamental building blocks. Therefore, counting graphlet frequencies is valuable for understanding structural characteristics and function of a given graph. In this paper, we propose an efficient algorithm CaTSCAN for counting the exact frequencies of typed graphlets of size up to 5 nodes in heterogeneous information networks, where the nodes of the graph (and graphlets) are assigned different types. Existing work has only addressed simpler problems, either focused on counting untyped graphlets of sizes up to 5 nodes, or in the case of typed graphlets, only considered counting graphlets with 3 and 4 nodes. CaTSCAN avoids excessive enumeration of individual graphlet instances by deriving the counts of larger graphlets from smaller ones with non-trivial and highly efficient combinatorics, while preserving type information. In an experimental evaluation, we show that CaTSCAN outperforms existing typed graphlet solutions on real-world datasets by up to 4 orders of magnitude for counting 3- and 4-node graphlets, and counts 5-node graphlets in less time than existing solutions count 3- and 4-node graphlets. CaTSCAN can even out-speed some untyped baselines on larger graphs.

source_records.title: Temporal Graph Classification Based on Fast and Exact Transitive Reduction Strategy
source_records.abstract: Temporal graphs are a variety of structured data that have been particularly studied recently. In this paper, we focus on classification of temporal graphs. Previous works have shown that such task can be tackled by first transforming temporal graphs to static ones using ad-hoc algorithms, before the classification step. However, resulting static graphs might be of huge size. Transitive reduction can be used to reduce the size and redundancy of such graphs, but with a high complexity time. In this paper, we propose a fully dynamic algorithm that transforms temporal graphs into static ones while applying exact transitive reduction at the same time. This algorithm has a much reduced complexity than doing both steps separately, while producing exactly the same output graphs. We show in the experimental section that similar accuracy is achieved for a lower computational time.

source_records.title: A Multi-heuristic Approach to Workload Placement in Virtualisation Environments
source_records.abstract: Dynamic resource allocation represents one of the core benefits of server virtualisation. Within a cloud computing context, a user issues an infrastructure request, which is satisfied by spawning one or several virtual machines (VMs). We argue that tearing down VMs once the initial request completes can prove sub-optimal. Indeed, this implies that for every new infrastructure request, the VM creation procedure is applied and, therefore, incurs the VM creation overhead. In this reseach, we consider workload placement as the first response to an infrastructure request, followed by a VM placement when no running VM has the capacity to execute the workload. Our solution proposes a multi-heuristic approach to workload placement in VMs. First, we employ a compound scoring function in the vector bin packing (VBP) algorithm to optimally assign workloads to running VMs. Next, the remaining workloads are placed on available VMs using a beam search (BS)-flavoured ant colony optimisation (ACO). We present an empirical evaluation with varied configurations to demonstrate that coupling VBP and ACO enhances the placement quality.

source_records.title: TimeAgent: From Matches to Memories—Timeline Summarization for Sports Analytics
source_records.abstract: Timeline summarization aims to condense evolving information across multiple documents into coherent chronological narratives. In the sports domain, this task is particularly challenging due to the volume of news and the need to focus on user-preferred attributes such as specific players or teams. While prior work has explored generic timeline summarization, datasets supporting attribute-aware timeline summarization in sports remain limited. To address this, we introduce MulSports , a dataset designed to facilitate research on attribute-conditioned timeline summarization for sports news. MulSports comprises 2,000 news articles spanning football, cricket, kabaddi, hockey, and volleyball, paired with extracted player and team attributes and human-written timeline summaries. Each instance associates temporally ordered articles with a target attribute, enabling evaluation of both attribute focus and temporal coherence. To illustrate the utility of MulSports , we present an empirical analysis using a simple multi-modular pipeline that integrates temporal retrieval with large language models. Experimental results show that fine-tuned models outperform prompt-based baselines. MulSports provides a foundation for studying personalized and temporally grounded summarization in sports. The code, datasets, and Appendix material are made available through an anonymous GitHub repository ( https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TimeAgent-277B/ ).

source_records.title: Part-GNN: A Partitioning-Based Graph Neural Network for Efficient Memory Large Scale Data Classification
source_records.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are a class of deep learning models that have demonstrated significant potential in various classification tasks, including image recognition and the prediction of labels for nodes and edges. Unlike traditional neural networks that operate on Euclidean data such as images or sequences, GNNs are specifically designed to handle non-Euclidean data, i.e. data represented as graphs, where relationships between entities are irregular and complex. These graphs may include rich node and edge attributes, making GNNs particularly suitable for domains such as social networks, molecular structures, and recommendation systems. Several GNN variants have been developed, including GCN, Cluster-GCN, GraphSAGE, and FastGCN. Despite their advantages, GNNs often require substantial memory, primarily due to the large adjacency matrices involved, which become computationally expensive for large-scale graphs. They also tend to have long training times. In this work, we propose a novel graph partitioning technique aimed at reducing the effective size of the graph while maintaining a high predictive F1-score. Furthermore, we integrate this partitioning approach with layer-wise training to enhance computational efficiency.

source_records.title: Design of a Query Expression for Multi-Dimensional Graph Warehousing
source_records.abstract: This study presents an extension of the conventional data warehouse query paradigm by introducing Multi-dimensional Graph eXpression (MGX), a multidimensional query framework designed to support Online Analytical Processing (OLAP) over graph-based business intelligence data. MGX extends the traditional Multi-Dimensional eXpression (MDX) syntax used in relational data warehouses by incorporating SQL-style analytical constructs, including GROUP BY, HAVING, and ORDER BY, thereby improving the expressive capability and flexibility of multidimensional analysis over graph warehouses. By bridging relational data warehousing technologies with graph-based analytical environments, the proposed framework addresses key limitations of traditional MDX in supporting graph-oriented analytics. It enables more effective exploration of semantically rich and socially connected knowledge embedded in networked datasets. Overall, MGX provides a practical methodological foundation for advancing graph warehousing and supporting next-generation network-centric business intelligence applications.

Body

Introduction A temporal network is a network whose structure and properties evolve over time. In the past decade, temporal networks have been used to model interactions between the components of complex systems with dynamic structures and characteristics. A temporal network consists of two key elements: a set of nodes representing components of a system and a set of links indicating interactions between pairs of nodes. In temporal networks, links between nodes may appear or disappear over time, and new nodes may also join. Broadly, temporal networks are represented in two paradigms: snapshot-based and continuous-time (event-based). Snapshot-based networks discretise time into intervals, yielding a sequence of static graphs, which is intuitive but may lose fine-grained temporal information. In contrast, continuous-time networks preserve the exact timestamps of interactions (events), enabling models to capture dynamics at arbitrary resolutions [ 1 , 2 ]. This distinction forms the foundation for most temporal representation learning approaches and is particularly relevant to temporal link prediction (TLP). Identifying the likelihood of connecting between nodes to predict future links in a network (link prediction) is a fundamental problem that can be applied to various domains such as social networks [ 3 ], telecommunication networks [ 4 ], traffic forecasting [ 5 , 6 ] or knowledge graphs [ 7 , 8 ]. Link prediction was first discussed in the context of static networks [ 9 ] where the aim has been to predict future links based on a network’s current state. In this paper this is referred to as traditional link prediction. However, TLP uses a network’s historical states to predict the likelihood of future links. Incorporating historical dynamics into the TLP problem introduces additional complexity [ 10 , 11 ]. In social networks for instance, such as the one shown in Fig. 1 , the TLP task is to predict the likelihood of a future link between User 1 and User 3 based on the observed temporal interactions among users. Fig. 1 Temporal link prediction in a social network Recently, numerous methods have been proposed to address the TLP problem, each method focusing on different network characteristics. Solving TLP requires two key ingredients: first, a representation unit , which models how a temporal network can be captured to reflect its traits and historical dynamics; and second, an inference unit , which determines the likelihood of future links based on the learned representation. Since all TLP models necessarily need both units, this review is confined to approaches concerning either representation or inference. Traditional surveys often categorise TLP models into broad methodological families such as “learning-based” [ 11 ]. This perspective provides a useful overview of existing approaches, but tends to emphasise overall model families rather than disentangling specific design choices. For instance, both TGN [ 1 ] and EvolveGCN [ 12 ] are typically labelled as “learning-based,” yet their underlying assumptions differ markedly: TGN employs a continuous-time message passing representation units with attention-based units making it effective for modelling of rapidly evolving interactions, whereas EvolveGCN adopts a sequence of discrete snapshots with RNN-based updates of GCN parameters, which is more suitable for gradually evolving networks. In the paper, TLP models are classified according to whether their primary contribution is to representation or inference; the defining attributes in each unit form the basis for the taxonomy adopted here. By separating representation and inference units, our taxonomy highlights such distinctions more explicitly, thereby clarifying how models align with different data characteristics and task requirements, and revealing unexplored combinations. The survey begins by examining various representation methods and discusses their merits and challenges. It then classifies and evaluates the inference approaches that have been explored in the literature. Guided by this methodological perspective, the discussion is subsequently divided into two sections “ Review of Representation Units for TLP ” and “ A Review of Inference Units for TLP ” dedicated to each unit, respectively. The survey highlights potential research opportunities through two primary avenues: (i) unexplored combinations of existing representation and inference units and (ii) the development of novel unit designs that could introduce new computational paradigms for either representation or inference. These opportunities could lead to more effective TLP approaches. Various surveys have been conducted to review TLP studies. Some surveys concentrate on specific network structures, such as homogeneous networks [ 13 , 14 ], or directed networks [ 15 ]. Other surveys focus on the application of TLP across various domains, encompassing temporal knowledge graphs [ 16 ] and social networks [ 3 , 17 , 18 ]. Our survey sets itself apart in several aspects: The survey introduces a novel taxonomy that distinguishes between the representation and inference units. Unlike existing surveys [ 13 , 14 – 15 ] which classify models under a single hierarchical framework, our approach separates these components to provide deeper insights into the models’ applicability and performance variations whilst also exploring diverse network characteristics pertinent to the TLP problem. The survey provides a comprehensive review of the representation unit. While previous surveys [ 3 , 17 ] provided some discussions of these models, we offer a systematic classification and analyse their ability to capture temporal and structural dynamics, thereby addressing a significant gap in the literature. The survey identifies current challenges and outlines potential directions for future research in representations, network characteristics, and TLP methodologies, offering valuable guidance for subsequent investigations in this field. Methods included in this survey come from papers identified using Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar and keywords on temporal networks, network representation and link prediction. Only articles written in English in the period 2000–2025 that propose relevant algorithms or methods were considered. The rest of this paper is organised as shown in Fig. 2 . “ Background ” presents the background on temporal graph representation and the problem statements. Following this, “ Taxonomy ” introduces the taxonomy framework. “ Review of Representation Units for TLP ” and “ A Review of Inference Units for TLP ” provide an overview of TLP methods, classifying them based on their representation and inference units. “ Variations of the TLP Problem ” and “ Future Research D

irections ” explore variations of the TLP problem and outline potential directions for future research. Finally, “ Conclusion ” presents the survey’s conclusion. Representation Methods Temporal graphs can be described using two distinct approaches for the time dimension: Discrete-time Dynamic Graphs (DTDG): A DTDG simplifies a temporal network into a sequence of timestamped snapshots, converting the continuous temporal space into discrete timestamps. This allows dynamic graphs to be represented in a static, analysable format, though some information may be lost between snapshots during discretisation. Summary This section introduced the foundations of temporal networks and the problem formulation of TLP. Temporal networks are modelled as temporal graphs, where the evolution of nodes, edges, and attributes can be described in either discrete-time or continuous-time paradigms, each offering different trade-offs between efficiency and information preservation. TLP extends traditional link prediction by requiring models to capture both spatial and temporal dynamics for forecasting future interactions. We further distinguished between transductive and inductive inference tasks, highlighting their respective assumptions and generalisation scopes. Overall, this background sets the stage for understanding the methodological developments reviewed in the following sections. In particular, the distinction between discrete-time and continuous-time representations, as well as between transductive and inductive inference tasks, provides the foundation for the taxonomy that follows. Taxonomy The Framework of the Taxonomy This survey proposes a taxonomy framework for TLP. It contends that all TLP methods comprise two sub-tasks: representing temporal networks and making predictions, which are processed by two distinct components: the Representation Unit and the Inference Unit. The representation unit captures the network structure and dynamics, whilst the inference unit leverages these representations to forecast future links. As depicted in Fig. 5 a, nodes, edges, and attributes are processed by a representation unit to produce inputs that capture dynamic patterns. Subsequently, the inference units process features or embeddings derived from the representation unit to infer future links. In [ 26 ], transductive and inductive tasks relate to inference units but not to graph representation. Direct inference is a prevalent approach in representation unit applications, whereby embeddings or features from dynamic network embedding methods directly yield predictions without requiring additional model training. Relationship of Representation Unit and Inference Unit As illustrated in Fig. 5 a, data are first transformed by the Representation Unit into features or embeddings that capture structural and temporal dynamics. These representations are then processed by the Inference Unit to produce link predictions, often in conjunction with auxiliary components such as candidate generation or negative sampling [ 1 , 81 ]. A TLP model, therefore, relies on the alignment between the expressive capacity of its Representation Unit and the predictive capability of its Inference Unit. For example, simple feature extraction in the Representation Unit, such as similarity or centrality measures, is typically paired with lightweight inference techniques such as time series models or distance-based scoring. In contrast, latent states derived from graph neural network encoders or continuous-time event-driven models usually require parametric inference modules, including multilayer perceptrons, recurrent decoders, or attention-based predictors. It is also important to note that many approaches to Representation Units and Inference Units are rooted in neural network architectures. Graph neural networks, recurrent networks, and attention mechanisms are different forms of neural computation that can be employed in either stage. Consequently, TLP models of

ten integrate these components in diverse ways, combining representation and inference modules into flexible and powerful end-to-end architectures. This neural foundation provides both strong approximation ability and architectural adaptability, allowing researchers to design models that are tailored to specific temporal settings while retaining the capacity to generalise across a wide range of prediction tasks. Temporal Graph Benchmarks In recent years, significant progress has been made toward standardising evaluation in temporal graph link prediction, most notably through the Temporal Graph Benchmark (TGB) [ 82 ] and its extension TGB 2.0 [ 83 ] on multi-relational and heterogeneous temporal graphs. These benchmarks provide datasets, unified preprocessing pipelines, and public leaderboards, 1 enabling systematic comparisons among a wide range of methods. TGB includes datasets from diverse domains. For example, a dataset on Wikipedia co-editing interactions focuses on predicting which page a user will edit at a given time [ 84 ]. Another dataset on Amazon product reviews considers the task of predicting the next product a user will review [ 85 ]. A financial dataset based on stablecoin ERC20 transactions requires forecasting the destination address of a transfer, including cases during the Terra Luna collapse [ 86 ]. A social media dataset constructed from Reddit reply dynamics predicts whether one user will respond to another [ 87 ]. Finally, a dataset on international flights predicts whether a flight will occur between two airports on a specified day [ 88 ]. Collectively, these datasets span domains such as collaborative editing, e-commerce, finance, social media, and transportation, highlighting the broad range of real-world applications for TLP. Both TGB and TGB 2.0 report systematic comparisons of TLP methods, ranging from classical heuristics and static baselines to state-of-the-art temporal graph neural networks such as JODIE, TGN, and CAW. The leaderboard results highlight that while sophisticated temporal models often achieve strong predictive performance, simple memory-based heuristics also remain competitive, especially on large-scale datasets. Summary Building on the distinctions introduced in the previous section, this taxonomy frames TLP methods around two complementary units: the Representation Unit and the Inference Unit. The Representation Unit reflects the discrete-time vs continuous-time modelling paradigm, focusing on how temporal networks are represented and encoded. The Inference Unit corresponds to the transductive vs inductive inference setting, determining how predictions are carried out given the learned representations. By combining these two dimensions, we categorise existing methods into four principal groups, providing a coherent structure for understanding these approaches. This design not only ensures consistency with the conceptual foundations of temporal networks but also highlights open challenges, such as bridging hybrid Representation and Inference Units, balancing representational fidelity and efficiency, and enabling models to generalise across diverse TLP scenarios. evidence_cards.document_title: A Survey of Link Prediction in Temporal Networks
evidence_cards.main_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive taxonomy of temporal link prediction methods, distinguishing representation units (snapshot-based, feature extraction, latent variables including Dynamic Graph Summarisation and autoencoders) from inference units (including RNN-based approaches). It systematically reviews how temporal networks are modeled as discrete-time dynamic graphs (snapshot sequences) and how graph summarisation, autoencoders, and recurrent neural networks are used for temporal graph representation learning.
overlaps: Models dynamic temporal graphs as sequences of snapshots (Discrete-time Dynamic Graphs, DTDG), matching the novelty point's feature of modeling dynamic sequential graphs as snapshot sequences
Discusses Dynamic Graph Summarisation (DGS) which collapses successive historical snapshots into a comprehensive weighted snapshot, overlapping with the graph summarization compression approach
Reviews autoencoder-based representation units (Dyn-VGAE, DynGEM, SDNE) for dynamic graph embedding, overlapping with the graph autoencoder component
Reviews RNN-based inference units (EvolveGCN, DynGraph2Vec, DDNE) for learning temporal dependencies, overlapping with the recurrent neural network component
differences: The survey is a review/taxonomy paper rather than a novel method proposal; it does not propose a unified framework combining graph summarization, graph autoencoder, and RNN in a single end-to-end architecture

The survey's DGS focuses on integrating historical snapshots into one weighted snapshot for link prediction, whereas the novelty point uses graph summarization to compress the original graph before feeding it into a graph autoencoder for representation learning
The survey does not specifically address training node representations of the original graph via reconstruction error with the original graph after graph summarization compression
The survey covers temporal link prediction as the primary task, while the novelty point targets general large-scale sequential graph representation learning
